texts: A research group is comparing two methods for serving a language model on a single accelerator. The first method processes one request at a time. The second keeps several requests active and adds a new token to each request on every scheduling step. Both methods load the same weights and use the same precision, but their memory access patterns can differ. Explain how batch size changes the number of times a weight matrix must be read per generated token. Include a separate discussion of attention keys and values, because their size grows with the prompt and generated sequence. A useful answer should distinguish a measured memory transaction from a tensor size calculated from model dimensions. It should also describe why a short prompt and a long prompt may have different latency even when the model has the same number of parameters. Finally, identify a workload where the arithmetic hardware becomes important enough that removing it would hurt throughput.

Review the following software design for a decoder benchmark. The program submits four prompts to an inference engine, starts a timer immediately, and divides the final elapsed time by the total number of generated tokens. It reports that number as pure decode latency. Some requests can finish prefill later than others, the engine may reuse a cached prefix, and the sampling configuration may stop early when an end token appears. Write a review that identifies each source of ambiguity and proposes checks that make the experiment reproducible. Specify what should happen before the timer starts, what must be recorded for every request, and how to keep the numerator consistent with the actual timed interval. Discuss why GPU event elapsed time and synchronized wall time answer related but different questions. The review should retain failed trials and token mismatches rather than hiding them in an average. It should also say which runtime version, model revision, precision, seed, and hardware identifier belong in the result manifest.

A city library is planning a small public exhibition about how maps changed over time. The curator has a table of paper atlases, aerial photographs, satellite images, and maps made from volunteer observations. Visitors range from school students to specialists, and many have never used geographic information software. Draft a short explanation of what each source can show and what it can miss. A paper atlas can preserve how people described a place in an earlier period, while a satellite image can reveal broad patterns at a particular moment. Aerial photographs often show more local detail, and volunteer reports can add street level observations that sensors miss. Explain why two maps of the same neighborhood may disagree without either one being dishonest. Mention scale, date, projection, sampling, and the choices made by a mapmaker. End with one question a visitor could ask when comparing a historical map with a current one.

Imagine a team maintaining a weather station on a remote ridge. The instruments record temperature, wind, humidity, and battery voltage every minute, but the radio link is intermittent. The station can store measurements locally and transmit them later. Write a practical plan for deciding whether an apparent temperature spike is a real event or a faulty reading. Compare nearby stations, check sensor health, and inspect the timing of the radio outage before drawing a conclusion. Describe how you would preserve the original measurements while adding quality flags and corrected interpretations in a separate record. Consider what happens if the battery voltage drops during cold weather or the sensor is exposed to direct sun for part of the day. Explain how to communicate uncertainty to a reader who wants a simple daily summary. Include one example in which the suspicious reading should remain visible even though it should not be used in the daily average.
